procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Additional Sessions Judge, Seoni, dated 18.07.2013, directing the release of a confiscated vehicle during the pendency of a criminal case.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State challenged the order of the Additional Sessions Judge by filing a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (M.Cr.C No. 12750/2013) before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur. The High Court dismissed the petition and affirmed the order of the lower court in an order dated 21.01.2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Aggrieved by the order of the High Court, the State approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition, which was converted into Civil Appeal No. 6112 of 2017.

issue.issue_text: Whether subsequent purchasers/assignees/power of attorney holders have locus standi to file a petition for a declaration of lapse of acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) of The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.

facts: The cases involved subsequent purchasers, assignees, or power of attorney holders of land that was subject to acquisition proceedings initiated under a prior law.
These proceedings had not been completed, as either compensation was not paid or possession was not taken for over five years.

After The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (the "2013 Act") came into force, these subsequent purchasers filed petitions seeking a declaration that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the new Act.
The acquiring authorities (appellants) challenged the right (locus standi) of these subsequent purchasers to file such petitions.
law: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act provides that land acquisition proceedings initiated under the old law shall be deemed to have lapsed if an award has been made five years or more prior to the commencement of the 2013 Act, but physical possession of the land has not been taken or compensation has not been paid.
There is an established legal principle that a person who purchases land after an acquisition notification has been issued is not competent to challenge the validity of the acquisition proceedings.
The 2013 Act aims to protect the interests of "persons who are interested in compensation/land owners/affected persons."
application: The Supreme Court first distinguished the nature of the legal challenge. It clarified that the subsequent purchasers were not challenging the legality or validity of the original acquisition proceedings.

Instead, they were seeking a declaration that the proceedings had lapsed by the operation of a new law, Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act. Therefore, the established principle barring subsequent purchasers from challenging the validity of an acquisition did not apply.

The Court reasoned that subsequent purchasers, assignees, and successors in interest fall under the category of "persons who are interested in compensation/land owners/affected persons" as contemplated by the 2013 Act.
Since they have an indisputable interest in the land and are affected by the acquisition, they are entitled to seek a declaration regarding the status of that land.

The Court held that the declaration of lapse is "qua the land" (in relation to the land itself). As the subsequent purchasers have a clear interest in the land, they have the necessary locus standi to ask a court to determine its legal status under the new Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that subsequent purchasers lack standing. It held that subsequent purchasers, assignees, and power of attorney holders are considered 'affected persons' under the 2013 Act and therefore have the locus standi to file a petition for a declaration that acquisition proceedings have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether subsequent purchasers/assignees/power of attorney holders have locus standi to file a petition for a declaration of lapse of acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) of The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
appellant_arguments: The appellants cited previous court decisions which, while holding that subsequent purchasers have no locus standi to challenge the acquisition proceedings themselves, did protect their right to claim compensation as a 'person interested'.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not explicitly state the respondent's arguments. However, their position would have been to oppose the appellants' claim and argue that subsequent purchasers do not have the locus standi to seek a declaration of lapse.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Confiscation under the law is permissible even if the guilt of the accused has not been completely established.
obiter: Powers of seizure, confiscation, and forfeiture are vested in authorities to enable them to take effective steps for preserving forest produce, and these provisions have an overriding effect over other statutes and laws.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In all the decisions cited by the learned Senior Counsel for the appellants, which we have referred to above, this Court has protected the rights of the subsequent purchaser to claim compensation, being a person interested in the compensation, despite holding that they have no locus standi to challenge the acquisition proceedings.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the established legal principle distinguishing between a subsequent purchaser's right to claim compensation as a 'person interested' and their lack of locus standi to challenge the acquisition proceedings themselves.
why_appellant_lost: The court determined that seeking a declaration of lapse under Section 24(2) is a form of challenging the acquisition proceedings, not merely claiming compensation.

The precedents cited by the appellants, while protecting their right to receive compensation, explicitly affirmed the rule that subsequent purchasers have no locus standi to challenge the validity of the acquisition proceedings.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the court maintained the long-standing legal principle that subsequent purchasers cannot challenge the acquisition proceedings that were initiated prior to their purchase.
The court implicitly found that the right to claim compensation does not confer a right to question the continuation or lapse of the acquisition itself.
